impacts.caseName: Dental Monitoring SAS v. Align Technology, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Board's Penumbra framework—holding that Dynamic Drinkware's written description analysis does not apply under AIA § 102 to determine a reference patent's prior art date—is correct, and whether a reference patent can claim the filing date of its provisional application for prior art purposes without satisfying Dynamic Drinkware's written description requirement.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the PTAB's final written decision finding claims of the '409 patent unpatentable as obvious, remanding for reconsideration of whether a key prior art reference (Carrier) was entitled to its provisional application filing date under AIA § 102(d)(2). The court's resolution of whether Dynamic Drinkware's written description requirement applies under the AIA has broad implications for determining prior art availability in IPR proceedings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners benefit from a potentially narrower path for challengers to establish prior art dates, making it harder to invalidate patents in IPR proceedings by backdating reference patents to provisional filing dates without adequate written description support.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies relying on IPR petitions to challenge competitor patents may face greater difficulty establishing prior art status for references whose provisional applications do not fully support the relied-upon disclosures.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether claims directed to non-uniform constellations for digital communication systems are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated summary judgment of patent eligibility for certain claims of the '761 and '700 patents while affirming eligibility for claims of the '509 and '922 patents, affirmed the denial of JMOL on non-infringement and damages, and remanded for further proceedings. This decision provides significant guidance on § 101 eligibility for communications technology patents and the boundary between abstract mathematical concepts and patent-eligible inventions.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in the communications technology space benefit from the court's affirmance that certain implementation-focused claims involving non-uniform constellations are patent-eligible, supporting enforcement of standards-related patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies implementing industry standards face continued patent infringement exposure, and the partial vacatur on eligibility creates uncertainty about the scope of patentable subject matter for algorithmically-derived technology improvements.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an exclusive license agreement conveyed 'all substantial rights' in the licensed patents such that the licensee could sue for infringement without joining the patent owner, and whether the licensee's shift to an enforcement-only business model triggered a termination clause in the agreement.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal, holding that the exclusive license agreement between Texas A&M University and TexasLDPC conveyed all substantial rights, making TexasLDPC a de facto assignee entitled to sue without joining A&M. The court also held that TexasLDPC's shift to patent enforcement did not constitute cessation of business operations triggering termination. This decision clarifies the 'all substantial rights' test for exclusive licensees.
impacts.positiveImplications: Exclusive licensees—including licensing entities and patent assertion companies—gain greater ability to enforce patents independently without joining the licensor, providing more flexibility in patent monetization structures.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers lose a procedural defense based on standing/joinder requirements, and the ruling validates enforcement-focused business models, potentially increasing patent litigation from non-practicing entities.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the trial court erred in its methodology for assessing copyright infringement damages via a hypothetical negotiation, including its use of the 'book of wisdom' doctrine and assessment of non-compensatory damages against the government.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the trial court's decision to use a hypothetical negotiation to assess copyright damages for the government's unauthorized copying of TETRA software, but vacated in part because the trial court adopted a legally impermissible view of the book of wisdom and assessed non-compensatory damages against the government. The case provides important guidance on copyright damages methodology in government software licensing disputes.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software companies gain clarity that hypothetical negotiation is a permissible damages methodology for copyright infringement, even when an existing license agreement exists, potentially supporting higher damages awards.
impacts.negativeImplications: The ruling limiting book-of-wisdom evidence and prohibiting non-compensatory damages against the government may constrain damages recovery in copyright cases against governmental entities.

impacts.caseName: Enanta Pharmaceuticals, Inc. v. Pfizer Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a change from 'C2-C12-alkyl' in a provisional patent application to 'C1-C12-alkyl' in the non-provisional application constituted correction of an obvious typographical error, thereby entitling the patent to claim priority from the provisional and avoiding anticipation by an intervening disclosure.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment invalidating all claims of Enanta's '953 patent as anticipated by Pfizer's public disclosure of nirmatrelvir (Paxlovid). The court held that the change from C2 to C1 in the alkyl substituent definition was not an obvious typographical error, so the patent could not claim priority to the earlier provisional application filing date, making Pfizer's intervening disclosure prior art. This decision has major implications for pharmaceutical patent prosecution and priority claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: Generic drug manufacturers and competitors benefit from strict enforcement of priority claim requirements, making it harder for patent holders to retroactively correct disclosures to antedate prior art.
impacts.negativeImplications: Pharmaceutical and biotech companies face heightened risk that even minor discrepancies between provisional and non-provisional applications could result in loss of priority date and patent invalidation, requiring extreme precision in provisional application drafting.

impacts.caseName: Range of Motion Products, LLC v. Armaid Company Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Egyptian Goddess en banc decision improperly reframed the design patent infringement inquiry to focus on differences rather than overall similarity, and whether claim construction involving functionality in design patents presents factual questions for a jury.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied en banc rehearing of a design patent infringement case, with dissents arguing that the Egyptian Goddess framework has shifted design patent infringement analysis toward dissimilarity and improperly allows courts to resolve infringement at summary judgment. The denial, accompanied by substantial concurrence and dissent opinions, signals ongoing tension in design patent law but preserves the existing Egyptian Goddess framework.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the preserved framework that allows courts to resolve design patent infringement at summary judgment when the claimed and accused designs are sufficiently distinct.
impacts.negativeImplications: Design patent holders face continued risk that courts may focus on differences rather than overall similarity when assessing infringement, potentially making it harder to enforce design patents at the summary judgment stage.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the six-year statute of limitations in 28 U.S.C. § 2501 for claims against the United States in the Court of Federal Claims is subject to American Pipe class action tolling.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that the six-year statute of limitations in 28 U.S.C. § 2501 is not subject to American Pipe tolling, recognizing that a portion of its prior decision in Bright v. United States was implicitly overruled by the Supreme Court's decision in ANZ Securities. The case arose from bank investors who lost assets in GSE preferred shares during the 2008 financial crisis and sought to bring claims after the limitations period expired.
impacts.positiveImplications: The government benefits from certainty that the § 2501 limitations period is jurisdictional and cannot be extended through American Pipe tolling, providing repose from stale claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Investors and businesses pursuing takings or breach of contract claims against the United States cannot rely on American Pipe tolling from prior class actions to extend the six-year filing deadline, requiring earlier independent action to preserve claims.

impacts.caseName: T-Mobile US, Inc. v. KAIFI LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Circuit has appellate jurisdiction over a contract interpretation dispute regarding the meaning of 'survives the EPR' in a patent litigation settlement agreement, or whether the dispute is a state law contract question that does not raise a substantial patent law issue.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held it lacked subject-matter jurisdiction over a dispute about the meaning of a settlement agreement provision requiring an additional payment 'if any Asserted Claim survives the EPR,' because the dispute was fundamentally one of contract interpretation under state law rather than patent law. The court transferred the case to the Fifth Circuit. This clarifies jurisdictional boundaries for patent-related settlement disputes.
impacts.positiveImplications: Parties to patent settlements benefit from clarity that contract disputes over settlement terms will be resolved by regional circuits applying state contract law, potentially providing more predictable and commercially-oriented interpretation.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies may face uncertainty about which appellate court will resolve post-settlement disputes, and must consider at the drafting stage that patent-adjacent contract terms may be interpreted by courts less familiar with patent reexamination proceedings.

impacts.caseName: Otsuka America Pharmaceutical, Inc. v. Hetero Labs Limited
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly construed the weight-to-weight ratio limitation in a pharmaceutical patent claim by interpreting 'dextromethorphan' and 'quinidine' to refer to the active moiety rather than salt forms, and whether the court erred in waiving the Rule 65(c) bond requirement pending appeal.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the preliminary injunction blocking Hetero's generic competitor to Nuedexta but vacated the district court's waiver of the Rule 65(c) bond pending appeal. The court's claim construction holding—that the drug names in the weight ratio refer to active moieties rather than salt forms—has significant implications for pharmaceutical patent claiming and ANDA litigation. The bond ruling reinforces that Rule 65(c) bond requirements should not be casually waived.
impacts.positiveImplications: Branded pharmaceutical companies benefit from the claim construction supporting broader patent scope, and the preliminary injunction blocks generic competition during the remaining patent term.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic drug manufacturers face barriers to market entry, and the claim construction interpreting drug names as active moieties rather than salt forms could broaden patent claims in Hatch-Waxman litigation more broadly. The bond requirement vacatur also creates financial exposure for preliminary injunction movants.

impacts.caseName: Board of Regents of the University of Texas System v. Boston Scientific Corp.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Boston Scientific was entitled to judgment as a matter of law of invalidity for anticipation and non-infringement of patent claims directed to drug-releasing biodegradable fiber implant compositions used in drug-eluting coronary stent systems.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed a jury verdict finding infringement and validity of a patent on drug-releasing biodegradable fiber implants, holding that Boston Scientific was entitled to JMOL on both invalidity (anticipation) and non-infringement. The decision overturns a significant damages award in the medical device patent space and reinforces strict application of anticipation and infringement standards.
impacts.positiveImplications: Medical device companies benefit from the court's rigorous application of anticipation and non-infringement standards, protecting against overbroad patent claims on well-known technologies.
impacts.negativeImplications: University patent holders and licensors face increased risk of JMOL overturning favorable jury verdicts, particularly when prior art closely approaches the claimed invention.

impacts.caseName: VDPP, LLC v. Volkswagen Group of America, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court abused its discretion in dismissing a patent infringement complaint without leave to amend, awarding attorney fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285, and sanctioning plaintiff's counsel under 28 U.S.C. § 1927.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed dismissal without leave to amend, the award of $207,543.60 in attorney fees under § 285, and sanctions against plaintiff's counsel for pursuing a meritless patent infringement action. The decision reinforces courts' power to deter frivolous patent litigation through fees and sanctions, particularly where counsel implicitly agreed not to amend yet attempted to do so.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from strong precedent supporting fee-shifting and attorney sanctions in exceptional patent cases, deterring frivolous patent assertions.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent assertion entities and their counsel face significant financial risk from pursuing infringement claims that courts deem meritless, including joint and several liability for fees and sanctions.

impacts.caseName: Archroma U.S., Inc. v. Department of Commerce
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Commerce's regulatory 15-day deadline for domestic interested parties to indicate intent to participate in antidumping sunset reviews conflicts with the governing statute, which is silent on filing deadlines.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the Court of International Trade, holding that Commerce's regulation requiring domestic interested parties to indicate intent to participate in sunset reviews within 15 days of the notice of initiation is a permissible exercise of the agency's authority. The statute is silent on timing, and the regulation was the product of reasoned decisionmaking within Commerce's delegated power. This preserves Commerce's procedural framework for antidumping sunset reviews.
impacts.positiveImplications: Domestic manufacturers benefit from preservation of Commerce's structured sunset review process, which ensures timely continuation of antidumping protections against foreign dumping.
impacts.negativeImplications: Importers and foreign manufacturers face the continued risk that strict procedural deadlines in sunset reviews could lead to continuation of antidumping duties even when domestic industry interest is marginal.

impacts.caseName: Ridge Corp. v. Kirk NationaLease Co.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly granted a preliminary injunction based on the patent holder's likelihood of success on the merits of infringement of an insulated overhead door patent.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed and remanded a preliminary injunction in a patent infringement case involving insulated overhead doors, finding errors in the district court's analysis. The decision addresses the standards for preliminary injunctions in patent cases and includes claims of tortious interference based on patent enforcement letters sent to third parties.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from rigorous appellate review of preliminary injunction grants in patent cases, preventing premature exclusion from the market.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face higher barriers to obtaining preliminary injunctive relief, potentially allowing continued competition during the pendency of litigation.

impacts.caseName: Exelixis, Inc. v. MSN Laboratories Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the asserted claims of patents directed to crystalline cabozantinib (L)-malate salts had adequate written description support under 35 U.S.C. § 112(a), in an ANDA litigation involving the cancer drug Cabometyx.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's finding that the asserted claims of the Malate Salt Patents had adequate written description, upholding Exelixis's patents covering crystalline forms of cabozantinib malate used in the cancer drug Cabometyx. This decision reinforces patent protection for pharmaceutical polymorphic forms and salt patents in Hatch-Waxman litigation.
impacts.positiveImplications: Branded pharmaceutical companies benefit from affirmance of written description adequacy for crystal form and salt patents, strengthening protection against generic competition for drugs like Cabometyx.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic manufacturers face continued patent barriers to entering the market for cabozantinib-based products, as the court validated the patent holder's written description for polymorph claims.

impacts.caseName: TrackTime, LLC v. Amazon.com Services LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether claim limitations reciting 'executable program code configured to' perform specified functions in a mobile device patent should be treated as means-plus-function terms under 35 U.S.C. § 112(f), in light of the Federal Circuit's intervening decision in Dyfan, LLC v. Target Corp.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated and remanded the district court's indefiniteness ruling regarding the '978 patent, holding that the lower court's means-plus-function analysis warranted reconsideration under the intervening Dyfan precedent. The court affirmed the jury verdict of invalidity for the '638 patent. This decision refines the framework for when software claim terms invoke § 112(f), with significant implications for software patent validity.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software patent holders benefit from potential narrowing of when § 112(f) applies to software claim terms, potentially saving claims from indefiniteness invalidity.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies accused of infringement face renewed uncertainty about the scope of software patent claims as courts reconsider the means-plus-function framework.
